falas.txt: This is the Airbus A-three-eighty. The biggest passenger airplane ever built.
Two full decks. Room for more than five hundred people. Some of them even had showers.
Passengers loved it.
And in twenty twenty one, after only two hundred and fifty one airplanes, Airbus stopped building it.
Now look at the seven forty seven. Older. Smaller. Designed in the nineteen sixties.
Boeing built one thousand, five hundred and seventy four of them, over more than half a century.
So why did the old giant win, and the new one lose? The answer is hiding in the strangest part of the seven forty seven. The hump.
To understand it, we have to go back to a time when Boeing was sure the seven forty seven would fail.
It's the late nineteen sixties. Air travel is booming, and airports are filling up.
Boeing's answer is an airplane far bigger than anything flying. The first airliner with two aisles.
To build it, they need a new factory. It's still considered the largest building in the world by volume.
In January nineteen seventy, the first passengers fly it from New York to London.
But inside Boeing, almost nobody thinks this is the future.
The future is supposed to be supersonic.
Boeing is developing its own supersonic airliner at the same time. And many people in the company expect it to replace the seven forty seven within a few years.
So the engineers plan for that day. When passengers move on to faster jets, the seven forty seven should be easy to turn into a freighter.
And that one assumption shapes the whole airplane.
The best way to load big cargo is straight through the front. So the nose has to swing up, like a giant door.
But the cockpit is in the nose. And you can't open a door through the pilots.
So they move the cockpit up, above the main deck, and smooth a fairing behind it.
That's the hump. It's not there for luxury. It's there so the nose can open.
The supersonic airliner was cancelled. The backup plan became the most famous airplane in the world.
And for decades, nothing else was as big. Here's why.
Back then, a twin engine airliner had to stay within sixty minutes of an airport, in case one engine failed.
That makes crossing an ocean nearly impossible. So long flights belonged to airplanes with three or four engines.
And if you wanted to move a lot of people a long way, there was really one choice.
Airbus watched Boeing own that market for thirty years. Then it decided to go bigger.
The idea made sense. Air traffic kept growing. The biggest airports were running out of room.
You can't easily add runways. But you can put more people on every flight.
So in December of the year two thousand, Airbus launches the A-three-eighty.
A full length double decker, with a wingspan of almost eighty meters.
Airbus talked about a market for nearly twelve hundred very large airplanes. It was the biggest bet in the company's history.
There was one more problem. The airplane didn't fit.
Its wings are so wide that airports had to widen taxiways and rebuild gates, with boarding bridges tall enough to reach the upper deck.
In the United States alone, eighteen airports planned to spend more than nine hundred million dollars getting ready for it.
So before it carried a single passenger, the A-three-eighty could only go where an airport had been rebuilt around it.
Then came the wiring.
Each A-three-eighty has around five hundred and thirty kilometers of wires. About a hundred thousand of them.
The airplane was designed in four countries. And the teams were not all using the same version of the design software.
When the wiring arrived for assembly, some of the cables were too short. In places, by just a few centimeters.
You can't stretch a cable. The first airplanes had to be rewired by hand.
It delayed the program by about two years, and cost billions.
The delay was painful. But what happened to the engines was worse.
When Airbus chose its engines, they were the best available. Nothing better was on the horizon.
Three years later, before a single A-three-eighty was delivered, engine makers had new designs that burned about fifteen percent less fuel.
They weren't for the A-three-eighty. They were for a new, smaller Boeing. The seven eighty seven.
The giant was out of date before it carried its first passenger.
And remember that sixty minute rule? It was gone.
Engines had become so reliable that twin engine jets were now allowed to fly for hours away from the nearest airport.
In two thousand five, a twin engine Boeing triple seven flew non stop from Hong Kong to London, the long way around. More than twenty one thousand kilometers.
Two engines to feed and maintain, instead of four. For an airline, that changes everything.
It also changed the map.
The A-three-eighty was built for hubs. You fly to a giant airport, change planes, and continue.
It's efficient. Ten cities can be connected with just nine routes through a hub. Linking each one directly would take forty five.
But passengers don't want to connect. They want to go straight there.
And with efficient twins, airlines could finally afford to offer that. Smaller airplanes, more routes, no stop.
That left the A-three-eighty with one hard rule. It only makes money when it's full.
Around five hundred seats are easy to fill between two giant hubs. On most routes, they're not.
One airline made it work. Emirates took one hundred and twenty three of them. Almost half of all the A-three-eighties ever built.
It was also the only airline that kept coming back for more.
So when Emirates cut its last order in twenty nineteen, Airbus announced the end. The program had cost around twenty five billion euros, and it never earned that back.
But here's the part most people miss.
The seven forty seven lost that same fight.
The newest passenger version sold just thirty six airplanes. Airlines wanted twins there too.
As a passenger airplane, the seven forty seven was finished years before the A-three-eighty.
So why was Boeing still building them in twenty twenty two?
Because of the hump.
Lift the nose, and a seven forty seven swallows cargo that fits in almost nothing else. Long, heavy, awkward loads, straight in through the front.
That's what kept the line alive. More than a hundred of the last model were built as freighters.
By the end of twenty twenty two, about four hundred and fifty were still flying. All but forty four were hauling cargo.
Airbus planned a freighter too. It even had orders. But after the delays, the customers walked away, and it was never built.
And that's the real difference.
The A-three-eighty was designed for one future. Giant hubs, full airplanes, four engines. When that future didn't arrive, it had nowhere else to go.
The seven forty seven was designed by people who expected to be wrong. So they gave it a second job.
The feature that made it look strange is the one that kept it alive for fifty years.
The last seven forty seven left the factory in January, twenty twenty three. Number one thousand, five hundred and seventy four. A freighter.
The A-three-eighty isn't gone either. Production ended, but the airplanes are still flying, and it's still a passenger favorite.
So the A-three-eighty didn't fail because it was too big.
It failed because it could only be one thing.
And the seven forty seven survived because of a hump it was never supposed to need.
